name: map-i32
axis: i32-keyed hash map: insert, hit/miss lookup, iterate (VL's dedicated mono key rep)
n: n=200000 keys (i*7+3), r=100 lookup passes over a 2n probe array (40M lookups: 20M hit, 20M miss), 1 values() iteration
nPython: n=50000, r=100 (4x fewer keys and 4x fewer lookups; scales linearly in n)
notes: Deliberately the SAME loop skeleton as ../map-string with only the key type changed, so the pair isolates the cost of a string key from the cost of the shared map machinery (probe/resize/tombstones are literally the same code in VL). Structural notes: Python's `hash(int)` is the identity and the keys are an arithmetic sequence, so Python's hash is free AND perfectly distributed — it is the most-favoured side here. Rust's default SipHash-1-3 over a 4-byte key is the least-favoured. VL uses an integer mix (`fbI32HashMix`) and V8 keys the Map on the SMI. Also carries `toplevel.vl`: a byte-identical algorithm with every binding at module scope (wasm GLOBALs) instead of inside `main()` (LOCALs), to quantify the known globals-vs-locals cliff. MEASURED RESULT: no cliff. locals 1064ms vs globals 1127ms = 1.06x (min of 9, interleaved). A control probe outside the benchmark set agrees: a bare 300M-iteration scalar accumulate reads 132ms with function locals, 138ms with top-level code over module globals, and 135ms with a function body reading module globals — all within 5%. Either the cliff has been fixed in this working tree or it does not apply to wasm globals under wasmtime.
